speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DREW  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER COMMENT ON USE OF POST OFFICE MANAGERIAL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday at a time when debate was taking place on a motion presented by the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) certain discussion took place in connection with references to a report which had been made to that department. I raise this question of privilege because of the interpretation which has been placed upon the statement made by the Postmaster General by different newspapers and which might reflect in some way upon the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) and the manner in which this information came into his possession.
I might say that the comment made by the minister would appear to fully justify the interpretation placed upon it; but I see, for instance, a report in the Ottawa Journal under the heading "Postmaster Plays Host Unawares". Merely to indicate that that was the general impression, the other newspapers picked it up. I see in the Hamilton Spectator of Saturday, January 16, this heading, "Postmaster Cote Pained, Surprised..."
That refers to a statement made by the Postmaster General on Friday after the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace had made certain references to the contents of a report made to the department by J. D. Woods and Gordon. These are the words of the Postmaster General appearing on page 1175 of Hansard of January 15 and referring to the statements which had been made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace:
I think my hon. friend is a little unfair. After all, I opened the door of my office and he spent the whole day there.
Half humorously and half seriously one of the newspaper reports I read created the impression that a new member in his innocence had almost stumbled on information which had not previously been available. Certainly the information was not previously available but there was no question of his 83276-76
stumbling on it. Certainly there was no question of his using information that had not been available in any manner that did not justify its use. I think it would be most unfortunate if public impressions were left or taken from the Hansard record that there was the slightest impropriety or unfairness on the part of the hon. member.
I think that this is of sufficient importance that I should refer exactly to what took place. On Thursday, January 14, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, in an earlier discussion of this motion, said, and I quote from page 1119 of Hansard of that day:
I would suggest that if the minister feels so inclined he might be brave enough to let us have access to the Woods, Gordon report to which he has referred. As I understand it, that was a study of certain aspects of the operation of the post office, and I believe it has never been tabled in the house.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: MR. DREW  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER COMMENT ON USE OF POST OFFICE MANAGERIAL REPORT
speechtext: It was a managerial report. We only have a few copies, but if my hon. friend will come to my office I will be glad to let him see it.

He was not able to complete his investigation on his first visit and he sent a note to the Postmaster General, the original of which I have in my possession. Pursuant to that, the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) visited the offices of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) with a stenographer and in the presence of the secretary of the Postmaster General proceeded to dictate further notations from that report, all of which was known to the secretary of the Postmaster General and to the office staff. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has correctly described what took place. Here was a confidential report made to the minister in respect to the administration of his department. A member expressed some interest in it and the Postmaster General allowed him to see it. I think that most of us who have been here for some time do find it rather surprising that a confidential document having been made available to the hon. member in that way was then used, or

extracts from it cited textually in this house, without there being any indication to the minister that there was any intention to make such use of that confidential document.
As to the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that the document be tabled, that would be contrary to the general practice. It has always been the practice of governments to get all the information and advice they find it appropriate to secure for the better administration of the departments for which they have responsibility, and it has never been the practice to table those documents. They are not prepared for the purpose of being a subject for discussion in the house. The minister is responsible for the administration of his department and he is entitled to get expert advice as to how the administration can be improved. But it is not the report that can be the subject of debate in the house, it is the way in which the department is administered; and I do not think there is anything unfair in the suggestion of the Postmaster General that he was surprised that a confidential document, having been communicated in that way, should have been made the object of textual citation in a debate in this house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the discussions on a matter of this kind become part of the record of the house, I think I should point out that this is not a confidential document in the sense of a document that is under restriction on the ground of security or something of that kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And I would point out that I am unable to see any difference between this document and the Currie report, which was voluntarily tabled by the Department of National Defence last year. I recognize it has been contrary to the practice of this government to table these reports unless they are forced to do so in some way, but I think that practice should be changed and that report should be tabled and tabled forthwith.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a comment on this because-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. In the first place, If I may be allowed to say so, this question should have been raised by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. That should have been his question, but the Leader of the Opposition chose to raise it himself and I saw that the house was interested in his remarks and therefore allowed him to proceed. I figured that it did not make so much difference at this point since it was raised by the leader of the party to which the

hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace belongs. But, in correcting an impression left by a newspaper, one should not-it being a so-called question of privilege-do more than is necessary to make the correction. But the Leader of the Opposition suggested the report be tabled and in the very last moment of the debate we were not talking about the matter in which the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace was involved. The matter which was being debated was whether or not the report should be tabled. I think that is a question which could be raised at a later stage. I do not think we should interrupt our proceedings any longer for the purpose of discussing whether the report referred to should be tabled.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Just one moment. Mr. Speaker, I just want to make this observation, not to debate in any way the point you have made, but since this will become part of the permanent record of the house I would point out that what I am referring to is a question of procedure which affects all members, and my own submission is that it was an appropriate course for me or any other member to rise on the question of principle in regard to the propriety of using information obtained in the way the information was obtained on this occasion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is a point on which the Leader of the Opposition and I disagree at this time. Does the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) wish to speak?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I wish to refer to a question of privilege which I suggest is important since it affects the possible course of action of members in dealing with information of this type. It is in that connection that I think the position should be clarified, if not now, certainly at some future time, because my own connection with this matter is that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace came to me on the same day he went to the Postmaster General's office, and we discussed together the question whether or not it was proper for the hon. member to use in the house extracts which he might obtain from that report.
It is that aspect of the matter which I think is of importance to every hon. member. In the course of our discussion it was my suggestion that I certainly would follow this course myself unless some ruling or authority was laid before us which indicated that it was not proper. I suggested to him that unless the Postmaster General laid down some conditions under which he would permit the hon. member to see the report, or 83276-76 J
Privilege-Mr. Zaplitny unless the report itself were marked confidential, I felt that any hon. member who says in the house "I want to see a report", and is given access to that report, is entitled to repeat in the house what he finds in that report.
In view of what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said about some surprise being felt that a report made available under these conditions should be quoted from, I think this is a matter that hon. members are entitled to have threshed out. My own view is, as I have said, that unless there is a condition clearly laid down as to the terms on which the report will be made available, or unless the report itself is marked confidential, then an hon. member should be free to quote from it once he has seen it.

1.	What effect, if any, has the federal tuberculosis control grant had on the lowering of the tuberculosis death rate in Canada?
2.	What factors, if any, may have contributed to this decline?

1.	The moneys made available by the federal government under the tuberculosis control grant have made it possible for the provinces to expand more rapidly their existing services and to establish new services of various kinds where these are deemed desirable.
The death rate from tuberculosis has dropped from 37-3 per 100,000 population in 1948 to 17-1 per 100,000 population in 1952.
2.	(a) Early diagnosis through increased mass X-ray surveys, widespread hospital admission chest X-ray examinations, and increased use of B.C.G. vaccine.
(b) More and better treatment facilities such as provision of extra hospital beds, the free distribution of streptomycin and other

related drugs supplied to sanatoria, and the increased use of newer surgical methods of treatment.
All these factors have been assisted by the use of moneys made available to the provinces under the national health grants program.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to remove the 3 per cent limitation from the section which makes provision for the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this motion is one which is familiar to all members of this House of Commons. Indeed, I am sure that its terms are familiar not only to those who were here in the last parliament but also to the new members of the house, for it is a subject that is quite familiar to the people of this country from one coast to the other.
As hon. members know, in the Income Tax Act there is a provision which permits income taxpayers, under certain conditions, to make a deduction from their taxable income in respect of medical expenses. However, it is important to note the conditions under which that right is extended. In the main, those conditions are three in number. In the first place, only those medical expenses can be deducted which meet the definition of "medical expenses" set out in the Income Tax Act. In the second place, there is a ceiling as to the total amount of medical expenses that any one taxpayer can enter when filling out his income tax form. In the third place there is the condition that an income taxpayer can deduct only that portion of his authorized medical expenses which is in excess of 3 per cent of his gross income.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think it should be made clear that, although hon. members may have views on each of these three conditions that attach to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes, the resolution before the house this afternoon asks for
Income Tax Act
a change in only one of these three conditions. For my own part, I have no serious objection to the condition in the act having to do with the ceiling as to the total amount of expenses that one can claim as a deduction. That ceiling was raised in the budget of 1952 to the figures that are now in the act, and although there may be some members of the house who think the ceiling should be higher, I for one feel that that part of the provision respecting medical expenses is reasonable, and I do not suggest that the ceiling should be raised.
However, with regard to the definition of medical expenses I think that there is room for improvement, and despite the fact that I do not include suggestions respecting the definition of medical expenses in the motion before the house this afternoon I think the definition of medical expenses should be amended. At the present time that definition is such that it restricts a taxpayer mainly to amounts paid to doctors, dentists, nurses and hospitals, together with the right to include expenses for certain specified drugs. There are one or two other items that are included in the definition but there are many things that are not included. For example, at a time of illness many a family is faced with other expenses that can be quite substantial. The need for extra help in the home can be a very real medical expense occasioned by illness. The food budget can go out of line because 'of illness in the home. These matters are not taken into consideration at all when it comes to medical expenses for purposes of the Income Tax Act.
Likewise, spectacles and hearing aids are not allowed as medical expenses although a dentist's bill is allowed as a medical expense even though that bill may include the cost of dentures which it seems to me are comparable to spectacles or a hearing aid. I mention these shortcomings in the definition in passing so that I can point out that there is a field there in which something should also be done, and also so as to draw a line and make it clear that, so far as the motion before the house this afternoon is concerned, it asks for just one change in this section of the Income Tax Act. My motion asks that what is now known as the 3 per cent floor be abolished and that all medical expenses right from the first dollar up to the ceiling in the act be allowed as medical expenses for one computing his income tax at the end of the year.
Hon. members are, I am sure, quite aware of the history of this very important provision. The right to deduct certain medical expenses was first put on the statute books

Income Tax Act
in time to be effective for the calendar year 1943. At that time Mr. Ilsley, who brought it in, provided that only those medical expenses could be claimed which were in excess of 5 per cent of one's gross income. It was an acceptable provision to have, but we on the floor of the house soon began contending either that the 5 per cent floor should be lowered or that the floor should be wiped out altogether. As I have indicated before, we had a very interesting experience in connection with this matter in 1944. That year there was no proposal in Mr. Ilsley's budget speech or in his budget resolutions to do anything about the 5 per cent floor, but when we were in committee on the budget resolutions there were many requests from the floor of the house asking that the 5 per cent floor be either abolished altogether or at least reduced.
On that occasion we had support from all quarters of the house including very interesting and significant support from the present member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), and on one point from the hon. member who is now Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). At any rate, despite the fact that there had been no proposal to do anything about this point in Mr. Ilsley's budget speech or budget resolutions, he did respond to the representations made during the course of the debate and brought in a resolution later in the 1944 session which reduced the floor from 5 per cent to 4 per cent. It was one of those occasions few and far between when the government right during the course of the session made some concession to the arguments put forward on the floor of the house.
The 4 per cent floor remained at that level until last year. In the meantime some of us kept on arguing that just as 5 per cent was too high so 4 per cent was too high. We kept on arguing that the nature of medical expenses is such that they should be on the same basis as charitable donations and that they should be allowed deductibility right from the first dollar up to whatever limits are set in the act. For a number of years it was a case of a few voices crying in the wilderness until 1950 and 1951 when considerable support developed in the house for our contention that the 4 per cent floor should be wiped out. The high point in the support for the contention that the 4 per cent floor should be wiped out was of course reached on March 26, 1952, when my private member's motion, worded similarly to the one before the house today, was passed unanimously by the house.
I do not intend to take any time arguing about technicalities on which we have spent

time before. I recognize that my motion merely asked the house to express the view that the government should consider the advisability of removing the 4 per cent floor. I make the point, however, that that is all that a private member's motion can ask when money is involved, and I make the point that usually when the government allows a motion of that kind to pass it means that the government is favourably disposed to the substance behind that motion. Despite the unanimous support that the house gave to my motion on March 26, 1952, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who was Minister of Finance on that occasion, ignored that idea when he brought down the budget a short time later. As a matter of fact, not only did he ignore the express wish of the house that something be done about the removal of the 4 per cent floor, but he left the floor as it was and raised the ceiling. In other words, he did nothing to help the little fellow but did something to help the big fellow by raising the ceiling.
I pause, having referred to what happened on March 26, 1952, to remind the house that, in addition to the support we got away back in 1944 from the hon. member for Ottawa West and the present Minister of National Revenue, in 1952 we had the spoken support on the floor of the house of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry), the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) as well, of course, as the support of the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), who was then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. It is interesting to note that all those members who openly supported this important resolution are back in the House of Commons once again. I hope that their support for this proposition will be evident today as it was in 1952.
As I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, despite the stand taken by the house on March 26, 1952, to the effect that the government should give consideration to removing the 4 per cent floor, nothing was done about it by the Minister of Finance when he introduced his budget a few days later. Of course, that did not mean the end of this campaign so far as I was concerned. I put the same motion on the order paper the next year, in 1953, and it was again debated. On that occasion however, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will recall, the debate was rather short-lived. It occurred on January 12, 1953, and Hansard records that I made my speech arguing that the 4 per cent floor should be removed. Then the Minister of

Finance made a reply, at the end of which he simply moved the adjournment of the debate. I mentioned the hon. member for Greenwood because he was one of those who were rather shocked at the procedure being followed.
We objected to the action of the minister in moving the adjournment of the debate because that prevented others from speaking on this important question and prevented the house from taking a vote on the motion itself. We did our best to show our justifiable dislike for that procedure by forcing a vote on the minister's motion to adjourn the debate. The minister being on the other side, we lost that vote. I hope that course will not be followed today, but that the government will permit this debate to continue and will let the house make up its mind whether or not this motion should be passed. I hope we can count on the consistency of those members who supported the motion in 1952, and that they will support it again today. I hope all those members who helped make it a unanimous expression in 1952 will agree that this motion should be passed today.
I keep referring to the motion before us today as though it were exactly the same as the motion in 1953 or 1952. There is one significant difference. Despite the fact the Minister of Finance gave this debate a short life in 1953 by moving the adjournment of the debate, he paid some slight attention to the motion when he brought down the budget on February 19 of last year. As hon. members will recall, that was the occasion when cyclical budgeting brought the minister around to the idea of making certain tax reductions and certain concessions, for the election was not far off. He introduced a resolution lowering that 4 per cent floor to the figure of 3 per cent. It is the 3 per cent figure which will apply for the tax year 1953. In other words, when the taxpayers, in a month or so, start making out their income tax returns they will be able to deduct medical expenses in excess of 3 per cent of their gross income.
Well, that is good, Mr. Speaker. We are making progress. We started out with 5 per cent, then it was made 4 per cent and how we have it down to 3 per cent. It does seem strange that so many bites have to be taken to implement what, in my view, is unquestionably a matter of correct principle. I hope we will not have to wait for two or three more elections to get three more bites in order to remove the 3 per cent floor. Surely, it is time to face up to the principle in this matter and completely wipe out the floor.
Income Tax Act
One of the arguments that the minister keeps using against this proposal to remove the floor is that there is a certain average of medical expenses which people have to pay. In his view, income tax deductibility should be allowed only when medical expenses get above that average. I dislike referring again to a story I told once before. However, it is the minister's own story, and I think it is a good one. I think it drives home the point better than half an hour of argument. It is the story of the occasion when the Minister of Finance was in conversation with the late deputy minister of finance, Dr. Clark. Apparently Dr. Clark was saying something about averages, and the minister asked him if he had heard about the man six feet tall who had drowned in a body of water the average depth of which was only five feet. I think the minister's own story makes the point very well. These averages are no help to a person who has even the average expenses, let alone the person who has expenses far above them.
In addition to that, I suggest to the minister and to the government that they cannot continue using this idea about averages because as time goes on people are spending more on medical expenses than in years gone by. The manner in which we live may be responsible for that, or perhaps it is that medical science is developing and there are more ailments known with which doctors and hospitals can deal. Whatever the reasons, we are spending more. I suggest that the average portion of our expenses that Canadians are spending on health is going up all the time. Health is important, and it is a good thing that we should devote an ever larger portion of our income to the maintenance of good health. At the same time we are spending more, the minister is prepared to lower the exemption from 5 per cent to 4 per cent and then down to 3 per cent.
If the 3 per cent floor is based on average expenses, according to his reasoning he should be consistent and raise the floor instead of lowering it. I am mighty glad he has not thought of it, and I hope I have not put the idea in his head. The fact is that the argument really carries no further validity, in view of the fact the government has not given any figures to which to tie this reduction from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the arguments against this proposal, which were never valid, are disappearing one by one. I hope that in this session, even though it is three or four years before an election and the time when tax concessions are made, we will have recognition of this principle and that something will be done about the matter.

Income Tax Act
I have done this perhaps several times when I have raised this question, but I think I shall have to do it again. I have given a few examples to show what happens to a taxpayer, on the one hand, if he makes a certain contribution to charity, and on the other hand, what happens if he incurs that same amount of medical expenses during the course of a year. In both cases there are ceilings as to the amounts one can claim by way of income tax deductibility. But in the case of charitable donations, one is allowed, as a deduction, the first dollar one gives away, provided a proper receipt is obtained for it. In the case of medical expenses, however, one does not get the first dollar or the first ten dollars, in fact one does not get any dollars allowed until one gets above 3 per cent of the gross income.
Let us take the case of a married man without any children. Let us suppose it is a case where the Income is $200 a month or $2,400 a year. If that man has no exemption other than the statutory one, the total amount of tax he would pay for the year 1953 would be $72. That includes the old age security tax. I might add that throughout these examples I am using the rates which people will have to pay by April 30 of this year when they file their income tax returns for last year's income. Now, if that taxpayer has medical expenses during the course of the year amounting to $200 the tax saving he will receive against that $72 is $23.04. One arrives at that by taking 3 per cent of his gross income of $2,400, and then giving him a deduction on the portion in excess of that.
However, if this same taxpayer who would receive a saving of $23.04 in lieu of $200 medical expenses were to give away $200 to approved charities, the tax concession he would get for that in the year would be $36. I have no objection to the tax concession made in respect of charitable donations. But it does seem to me that the treatment accorded in respect of charitable donations made voluntarily should be the same treatment accorded to medical expenses made involuntarily.
Let me take the case of a married man with a wife and two children, having a total income of $300 a month or $3,600 a year. Let us assume in this case medical expenses of $300. If this couple did not have medical expenses or any other allowable deduction they would pay on their 1953 income at the end of April the sum of $240. For medical expenses of $300 they will get a tax concession of $38.40. But if they gave away to approved charities the same amount of $300 their tax concession would be $60. This couple is given $60 by

way of tax relief for giving away $300, but a concession of only $38.40 by way of tax relief if they have to pay $300 in medical expenses.
Bear in mind that no question is raised as to the average amount people give away to charities; that deductibility is allowed right from the first dollar. But in the matter of medical expenses the question of the so-called average is raised.
Let me go on and take another example. In this instance I shall work it out for a married couple with two children, and an income of $5,000 a year. In that case the gross tax is $537.50. If they had medical expenses of $500 in the year they would get tax relief of $78.75, but if instead of medical expenses of $500 in that year they had made charitable donations of the same amount they would have tax relief of $112.50. Let me repeat those figures: $112.50 tax relief if they give away $500 but only $78.75 if they are faced with the necessity of paying medical expenses to the same amount.
Then let me go down the scale again to the married couple with two children and an income of $200 a month or $2,400 a year. In that instance their gross tax, without any special deductions, would be just $18 a year. Let us suppose that they have medical bills in that year amounting to $100. The tax saving given on that $100 is only $5.04; but if they gave away $100 in the year the tax saving would be $18.
Again let me take the case of a married couple with two children and an income of $3,000 a year. In that instance the gross tax would be $126. If they have medical expenses of $100 a year their tax saving because of this 3 per cent floor would be only $1.80. But if they gave away $100 in the year their tax saving would be $18, ten times as much.
Depending upon the examples, the relationships differ. However, I draw particular attention to this example, using figures which I suggest are not uncommon. I refer to the couple with two children and an income of $3,000 a year, with $100 to be paid either as medical expenses or by way of charitable donations. Yet, because of that 3 per cent floor, this family would get ten times the tax relief for the contribution of $100 that it would get for the same expenditure by way of medical expenses. It is only $1.80 in one case but $18 in the other.
Without going into detail, the married couple with a salary of $3,000 a year and with four children, spending the same amount of $100, would be treated in exactly the same

way-$1.80 tax relief for $100 of medical exenses but $18 tax relief for $100 charitable donations.
It seems to me that the unfairness of this floor, and what it does to the taxpayer with medical expenses, as compared with what it does to the taxpayer who makes church and charitable contributions must surely be obvious to everyone. It has been obvious to members in the past. It was obvious in the debates prior to 1952. I know many members spoke to me in those days and suggested that this was a case that surely should be met by the government. It was obvious to members in 1952 when they supported the motion calling upon the government to consider the removal of the floor, and certainly it was obvious to the people of Canada that this change should be made, because it was a matter of considerable interest in the press-and particularly in that year when the house expressed its view, and when the government flew in the face of that view.
I urge the house on this occasion to give its approval once again to the motion. And this time I hope when that has been done the government will take that expression of opinion on the part of the house much more seriously than it did in 1952. In fact, I think it should be taken more seriously than it was in 1953 because, although the minister did something in that year when he reduced the floor from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, it must be remembered that that action was taken on the eve of an election. And, even so, it was not good enough.
Not only do I contend for the resolution on the ground of its essential fairness, which I think is borne out by the comparative treatment I have indicated as between medical expenses and charitable donations, but for the other reason I have already indicated, namely that medical expenses as defined in the act do not cover all the bills that hit a family when there is illness in the home. I could refer to some of the other things that are not covered, and make special mention of glasses and hearing aids. I have referred also to the extra cost of help when illness strikes in a home. I would be the first to recognize that it would be pretty hard to work out a definition that would really cover everything, and I recognize in particular the problem with respect to extra help. I understand it might be argued that in some cases such help was really necessary while in others it was not, but that a person of some means might want to spend money in that way.
Income Tax Act
As I say, I will be the first to recognize these points. But the very fact that you cannot work out a definition that will cover all medical expenses makes it all the more urgent that the medical expenses that are defined, including payments to doctors and hospitals, and the like, should be allowed right from the first dollar. I know of few issues which come before the house in connection with which justice and fairness indicate so clearly what should be done.
Another example of the failure of the present provision to fill the bill has to do with drugs such as insulin. A few years ago when the minister broadened the definition of medical expenses allowable under the act he included insulin and made a great to-do about it as well. I could bring to this house a good many letters from users of insulin who wondered at all the fuss. The fact of the matter is that although they are faced with a heavy cost for insulin during the course of the year, because of what was the 4 per cent floor and is now the 3 per cent floor they find they do not get to that floor or they do not get very far over it, so in many, if not in most cases, that provision for that particular drug is just so many words in the act. It does not mean anything to the persons who are really affected.
The same applies to some other drugs that are mentioned in the act, not to mention the fact that in my view there are still other drugs that have not been included in that definition and which as I see it certainly should be.
Another reason why I contend that this motion should be passed by the house and its substance acted upon by the government is that it moves in the direction in which society is thinking these days. I for one want to make it perfectly clear-perhaps I do not need to as this house knows me well enough-that even if this motion were passed it would not be the last word from me or from this group on matters of health. This is just a drop in the bucket; this is just a small step in the right direction. There is no doubt about it that we want to go on to a program of adequate health insurance and health coverage for the people of this country. It is because it is a step in that direction that I feel the government should at least move that way.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has got to the point where he not only dislikes my questions about health insurance, he will not give me an answer in substance, or he has even forgotten the number of times he has said that. The fact of the matter is that no less a person than the Conservative minister of health in

Income Tax Act
the province of Ontario thinks that within five years we will have health insurance or at least hospital insurance covering every person in Canada.
I commend that to my good friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor), who does not share my views on this question, who thinks that this party has too much to say about health insurance. In fact I will pass this clipping over to him right away which shows what the Ontario minister of health thinks on that question. The hon. member for Winnipeg South says that Dr. Phillips does not say how he is going to bring it about. It is true there are problems to be worked out, but I give that as an example from the extreme right in this country of the way Canadians are thinking. The fact is accepted that the care of the health of the people of this country is something of extreme importance and that more and more we have to make the necessary changes in our economy to take care of the health of the people of this country.
This move that I am proposing is just a little drop in the bucket. But because it is a step in the right direction, because the people of the country have become aware of the unfairness of the 3 per cent floor, I urge that the government delay no longer in taking action on this important question.
As I say, the arguments against it have in my view been pretty well set aside. The argument about allowing only those expenses which are above the normal or above the average is, as I have suggested already, really quite fallacious. I think the minister's story to the late Dr. Clark really sets that aside. So far as any individual person is concerned, if he is hit with heavy medical expenses it is no comfort to tell him that that is just the average, that that is just normal. It is certainly no comfort to tell him that if he had- not been hit with that expense and had given that amount away to charity he would have received better treatment from the income tax people.
Another argument that the government has used from time to time is that it would cost a certain amount. Certainly a -cut in taxes costs money just -as the imposition of a tax raises money. The whole point of any income tax structure is that it should be fair. To say that there is $30 million or $40 million which the government would not get if the floor were wiped out is no excuse for keeping on the floor. That $30 million or $40 million should be made a challenge to the government to find some fair way in which to raise that amount of money.
There was one occasion when the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) suggested,
iMr. Knowles.]
although I think we cleared the ground between us at least-I mention this in case anyone else wants to use the argument- that we should not go too far with this idea lest we provide too much help for wealthy people. It is always interesting to note the way in which that argument is used. I simply point out that the possibility of wealthy people gaining tremendously or gaining substantially as a result of the removal of this floor is nullified by the ceilings that are in the act. I have no objection to those ceilings. It is not going to be possible when you take away the 3 per -cent floor for the rich man to get his doctor to prescribe a trip to Florida and charge it as medical expenses. I suggest that that argument does not apply at all.
This request that I am making is, in the words of the hon. member of Spadina (Mr. Croll) in one of the debates on this matter on a previous occasion, a measure to help the little fellow. In view of the wide support that this measure has had across the years in the country; in view of the wide support it has had in this house, particularly the unanimous support that was given to it in 1952, I urge the house to pass the motion on this occasion.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate my support for the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I have supported the same or a similar resolution on occasions before this and have indicated personally my reasons for so doing. The case submitted by the hon. member who has just spoken is pretty complete and does not need too much argument to support it. I think the hon. member has shown quite clearly that there are good and sufficient reasons why the government should listen to the members of the house and remove the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses forthwith. The reasons given by the hon. member, as I recall, were the following.
In the first place, we are doing something for the little man. I agree with that. I do not know of any better way of doing it in connection with budgetary matters than to relieve him of the necessity of paying income tax on medical expenses. I have every respect for the claim of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that he is charged with the responsibility of distributing the tax burden fairly. That is quite true, but my own feeling is that he is not distributing the tax burden fairly if he imposes upon the little man the necessity of paying income tax on expenses in connection with medical expenditures within his own family.

The second reason given by the hon. member was that the removal of the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses would then be placing deductible medical expenses on exactly the same basis as contributions to charitable institutions. I see no reason why that should not be done. If we are going to be fair about it a person should receive the same consideration for medical expenses as he receives for contributions to charitable institutions. I believe that that is a good, sound argument.
The third reason given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was that there is widespread support for it throughout the country and that the principle is fair and just. Certainly I can say that there is widespread support for the removal of this 3 per cent floor on medical expenses in my constituency.
My people have asked me to repeat that this is so, and during the last tour I made of the Peace river country people conveyed to me their desire that I speak in support of the removal of the 3 per cent floor, as we have done on other occasions. I think that since the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made such a good case for the removal, I should take time perhaps to supplement that by dealing with some of the arguments used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on January 12 last. The hon. member has, I think, dealt with these to some extent but there are two or three comments I would like to make in addition. I do not want to amplify my comments on this resolution because I think it is important that we keep our speeches as short as possible so as to make it possible for a vote to be taken in the house today.
The minister, speaking I think on the same subject at a time when the Income Tax Act adjustments were before the house, on January 12 last, had this to say as reported at page 900 of Hansard for 1952-1953:
It is all right to pass resolutions couched in these terms, relating to budget matters, if it is understood that they do indicate what they say, in the terms indicated, namely, that the government should give consideration to certain matters. But the ultimate responsibility as to the fairness and the desirability of making these budget changes must rest with the government.
Now, the minister by these words was complaining against the impression that had got across the country in the minds of the people that this house having unanimously passed a resolution in 1952 to the effect that the 4 per cent floor as it then existed should be removed, it was incumbent on the government to take action and remove the 4 per cent in the budget. The people rightly got the impression that that was what should be done, and the people of Canada took it for

granted that when there was unanimous approval of a resolution in this house the government would pay attention to it.

I understand, but that is not what was in the minds of all the members who were debating the problem on the floor of this house. What was in the minds of the members when they debated the resolution was that the government ought to remove the 4 per cent floor. It is all very well to sit back and say that all you agreed to was that consideration would be given to it, and that consideration was given to it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize this very important point. It is the attitude of the government that I do not like, as expressed in these very words. It is the same attitude that Mr. Ilsley, the former minister of finance, gave expression to in this house on a certain occasion when he was confronted with the fact that while the house was in session certain orders in council had been passed, and when we took him to task for it I well recall with what indignation and heat the minister pounded his desk and said, "I want hon. members to know the executive council does not get its power from this house. It gets it from the crown." It is that attitude carried over into a resolution of this kind that we take exception to. I suggest that when members of this house, representatives of the people, unanimously pass a resolution to do a certain thing, then the government ought to take that into consideration and see that something is done. They should not sit back and say: "It is our duty to give consideration all right, but we are the ones who will say whether action shall be taken".
If we are going to have real democracy in this country, then that means there must be government according to the will of the people. If we are not competent, as members representing the people, to express their will, and only members of the cabinet are competent to express will, then I would ask what kind of government that is. It certainly is not a democratic government and I think it is about time we began to pay some attention to the expressed views of the people of this country and particularly of the members of this house who represent the people when they unanimously vote for a certain thing or a certain objective. I think it is high time the government paid strict attention to a vote of that kind and proceeded to carry out its intentions instead of complaining that that sort of resolution should not be passed.

Income Tax Act
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the government will not take the same view this year and put a block in the way of a vote on this resolution; or, on the other hand, rally the support of the members good and true of the Liberal party, the boys who at the crack of the whip vote the way they are told to vote and see to it that the resolution is voted down. There was a unanimous vote in this house in 1952 on this matter when the floor was 4 per cent, not 3 per cent. The minister last year brought in a budget that reduced the floor to 3 per cent and to that extent it was a move in the right direction. But it certainly did not do what the house gave the minister instructions to do by that unanimous vote. I suggest that the minister's argument is pretty weak. At any rate he is simply repeating what Mr. Ilsley repeated, that the executive council does not get its instructions from the House of Commons but takes them from the crown. Where is the crown in this case?

Well, of course, that is out of the question. I want to deal just a moment with another matter in this connection. The minister bolstered his argument for failing to remove the 4 per cent floor by using these words, that the philosophy behind this, that is retaining the floor, is that it is quite within the capacity of the ordinary individual to pay the normal expenses incurred for normal medical care or attention, but when this is beyond what can be considered as a normal amount, then and then only should there be special relief.
That is a specious argument and it certainly must have occurred to the minister in his calmer moments that it was so, because he already recognizes the principle of granting exemptions from the very first dollar on for certain living expenses. He gives exemption to single taxpayers in this country of an amount up to $1,000 on income and for married people up to $2,000 of income. Why? Because he figures it requires $1,000 to pay the normal living expenses of a single man and $2,000 to pay the living expenses of a married person. He recognizes the principle and then turns around and says that he has to recognize that there are certain normal expenses which everyone should be asked to pay and therefore it will be only the amount above this normal expense that he could recognize as being deductible for income tax purposes. His argument does not hold in any way whatsoever, and I suggest he is on much sounder ground when he resorts to a third argument, that if he should abolish the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses he will lose a certain amount of revenue. I

think he is on pretty sound ground there because I think it is fairly well established that the removal of the 3 per cent might mean a loss of as much as $40 million in revenue. I think perhaps it could be shown the amount would run to that figure. That may not be, but at any rate there will be a fairly substantial loss. But, Mr. Speaker, if it can be shown-and I suggest that it can and already has been shown-that it is fair and just for the government to remove the 3 per cent floor, then I say that the Minister of Finance should go ahead and remove it; and if it requires the sacrifice of $30 million or $40 million of his revenue, I suggest that he make it up by increasing the rates of taxation on those incomes over $5,000. Then he would be covered. He would be far better justified in doing that than he would be to leave this S per cent floor as it is. I suggest that there is every good reason why this is the time to remove the floor and to put the taxpayers of this country on the same basis with respect to medical expenses as they are on with respect to contributions to charitable institutions.
I think I have probably said enough about the matter at the moment, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that I am in complete support of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles); and I will just let the matter rest at that.

Mr. Speaker, I have not very much to add to what has been said. I should like to say a few words about the history of this resolution which is somewhat more interesting than that of most resolutions that come before us. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has made the argument very fully, as he always does. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has done full justice to the argument that the government entirely disregarded a unanimous vote of this house. It is only fair to say that at the time that was done the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, now the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), in his usual breezy way outlined what was being done and what was not being done by the resolution. This is what he said as reported at page 822 of Hansard of 1952, and I would ask the hon. member for Peace River to listen to this carefully because it has to do with what he has just said. These are the words of the Minister of Fisheries:
... I should like to say that the Minister of Finance accepts this resolution for consideration the way he accepts every letter or brief or interview put forward by any group in the country at this time as a proposal that he should consider in the preparation of his budget which will be delivered to this house on the evening of April 8.

Later on I shall have occasion to point out that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre agreed with this situation. Of course it is extremely unflattering to the members of this house to realize that a unanimous vote of this house is given just the same consideration-neither more nor less-as any letter or brief or interview put forward by any group in the country. That is not very flattering to us. Let us take, for instance, the chamber of commerce of Aklavik which, as I understand, is now on the move and possibly their deliberations would not be as careful as they might otherwise be. But at any rate, we have the satisfaction of knowing that our representation was to receive-and I have no doubt it did receive-the same consideration as do all the others which have been mentioned. How much or how little that was, we do not know. I spoke briefly of what happened just as the vote was being taken because it was made very clear to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who, as reported at page 828, said:
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I realize lull well that the passing oi this resolution does not mean the immediate legislative enactment of what it asks for.
That certainly was an understatement. I continue to quote:
The resolution asks for all that a private member, under the rules of this house, can ask for, namely that the government give consideration to the proposal that the 4 per cent floor in connection with medical expenses in relation to income tax should be wiped out. I take it that if this resolution is passed, since it has won the support of the government, the government will do what the resolution asks . . .
Later on the same page the Minister of Fisheries says this:
I must make this correction. What the house is voting on is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) should give consideration to this proposal.
And the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre added "That is right".
In looking at this situation, notwithstanding that the impression I think we carried away and the expectations that we naturally entertained were disappointed, nevertheless I think we must realize that technically the situation at the moment was made clear.
I refer next to what happened on January 12, 1953. Looking back I suppose we can say now that in 1952 the government probably let the discussion go a little bit further than perhaps it intended to or a little bit further than it felt, in retrospect, was wise. I think the Minister of Fisheries himself would have done it infinitely better than I did it. It was a poor performance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being private members' day I intend to exercise my prerogative as a private member to speak on this resolution, and I am glad to join my Conservative friend who has just taken his seat in supporting this silk hat socialist legislation. The subject matter is not a new one, and I often wonder why members sitting on the government side of the house allow so much time to be wasted on a matter that is so small. In my opinion the removal of the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses is a very small matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in presenting his last budget, pointed out to us that in the lower income brackets there were more than
136,000	families in this country who did not pay taxes. Therefore the number in the lower brackets who would benefit from this proposal is not as great as we might think.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the other members who have just spoken have gone into that side of the question rather fully, and I am not going to repeat what they said. I agree with their arguments. But it is not the 3 per cent floor that worries me so much as the definitions in the act. The amount that one spends on medicine is not deductible and that is something that affects everybody. The angle with which I am going to deal is that moneys paid for health insurance to doctor and hospital schemes are not allowed as deductions for income tax purposes. I am going to take an example close to home, but it applies generally. I want to refer to the contributions that mine and steel workers make to doctor and hospital plans in the part of the country in which I live. The individual contribution amounts to $117 per year and covers complete hospital and medical service.
But the only reason that any of the present schemes are able to function at all is by virtue of the large number contributing to such insurance plans who never receive any benefits from them. Otherwise such schemes could not work. I have made payments to one for about 45 years. It is very seldom

that I have ever consulted a doctor, and I have never occupied a bed in a hospital. There are thousands more like me. If there is a charitable contribution made by anyone in this country it is the contributions made to these insurance plans by those who do not receive anything from them which enable the provision of the services of hospital and doctor for those who need them. On that basis it is certainly a charitable contribution.
On former occasions I have asked the Minister of Finance to consider allowing as deductible for income tax purposes the money paid into recognized doctor and hospital plans in any part of the country. I have no hope that this resolution will pass, but it does provide a chance for members to get up and analyse the problem, and I hope that the minister will give consideration to the different views presented when he is again preparing his budget. The allowing of such payments as a deduction is one thing I want him to think about.
Another point to which I think some consideration must be given has to do with the large amount of money paid by families to drug stores year by year. It is a direct medical expense. In many cases there is a prescription ordered by a doctor. Drugs cost a great deal. Take aureomycin, for example. A man goes to a doctor, is examined by him, and the doctor says that he needs some of these pills. They cost $1 each. The man pays for them but because he purchases that medicine from a drug store he is not permitted to deduct the cost. I am safe in saying that the greatest expenditure that the average low income group family makes in the course of a year so far as health is concerned is the amount of money it spends for drugs in the corner drug store. I think people should be permitted to keep track of such expenditures and allowed to deduct them as a medical expense.
There is also the question of hearing aids which may seem very simple. But the man who has a hearing aid really needs it or he would not buy it. There is not only the initial expense of buying the hearing aid. It must be kept in repair month by month. When it is brought in from the United States in the first place it is taxed. It is quite costly. Then the person has to purchase batteries for it month by month and other little odds and ends in order to keep the equipment operating. In the course of a year a person who has to use a hearing aid will spend quite a little bit of money in keeping it running. I think the minister should give consideration to allowing such expenses as an offset against income tax.
Income Tax Act
Then there is the question of the man with an artificial leg. He has to buy it, and over the years a great deal of repairs enters into the maintenance of an artificial leg. If he lives in my part of the country, and I suppose the same is true of the western provinces, he has to ship the leg to a regular orthopedic centre in Toronto to be repaired, and such repairs are costly. That is another consideration for a man who is already handicapped by having to wear an artificial limb and provide for its maintenance year by year. Certainly, such a medical expense should be allowable as a deduction from income tax.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
It is
true, as hon. members have pointed out, that this is at least the third session at which the house has had an opportunity to debate this motion. Last year the views of the government were presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who is unavoidably absent at the moment. He informs me, however, that the views he expressed in Hansard for January 1953 are those that he has today.
Something has been said about the phrase in the resolution that the government "give consideration" to this problem. If, under our rules, that were all that could be read into the resolution, or if the conduct of the members of the opposition on other occasions had been different, probably the course which was adopted in 1952 could be followed today. We have approximately 70 new members in this first session of this parliament, and I think that they would probably be anxious to have some information as to the significance of a motion of this kind.
Before referring to events that took place in 1952, in a rather different way from some of the members of the opposition so far, I should like to have something to say concerning the history of this particular section of the Income Tax Act. As has been stated, it was introduced as a new form of deduction in 1942. There was a very good reason for this which has not been fully stated. In looking up the record, hon. members will find that this particular form of deduction was not introduced as a result of any pressure or in fact any suggestion from members of parliament, let alone the opposition members. In 1942 the administration realized that, in consequence of the very high rates of taxation existing at that time, certain taxpayers, faced with unusual and extraordinary medical expenses, would not have remaining with them funds adequate to take care of them and also their normal living expenses and their taxes.
I think that would be fairly evident if I were to remind members of the rates of taxation existing at that time and give some idea as to how 1942 taxes compare with the income taxes applying in 1954. In 1942 a taxpayer with single status had an exemption of only $660 as compared with an exemption in 1954 of $1,000. In the case of a married taxpayer the exemption in 1942 was only $1,200, whereas today it is $2,000. In the intervening years another new form of exemption has been introduced. This has particular significance when we are considering the problem of medical expenses.

An extra exemption has been given to the elderly in our community. Taxpayers over 65 years of age are now provided with an exemption of $500 in addition to the normal exemptions which I have indicated. To an extent this was provided because it is recognized that people of that age probably have unusual expenses, for example medical care, beyond those of younger people.
I would also like to give some comparisons to the house of what income remains in the hands of taxpayers now after paying their taxes in comparison with taxes and the compulsory savings called for in the war year of 1942. A married taxpayer with no dependents in 1942 with an income of $2,500 paid a tax, including compulsory savings, of $651. That same taxpayer today with an income of $2,500 pays only $75 plus $10 for his old age security tax.
A taxpayer married but without dependents in 1942, on a salary of $3,000 was required to pay in tax and compulsory savings the sum of $884. That taxpayer today is required to pay $150 plus $20 to provide for old age security. 1 am sure some members in the opposition would immediately raise the point that there has been a certain decrease in the purchasing power of the dollar in those intervening years. They might say that the take-home or the left-over pay after taxes in 1954 has not the purchasing power it had in 1942. Let us admit that, and then look at the consumer price index projected back to 1942. Doing this we find that the cost of living since 1942 has increased 59J per cent. But, looking also at the average weekly wage in 1942, we find that those average weekly wages have risen 100 per cent. Therefore when one compares the left-over income after paying taxes in 1942 as compared with 1954, on an income of $2,500 of a married man without dependents we find that in 1942 it was $1,849 while in 1954 it is $2,415.
Then, despite the warning of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about using averages, if we can assume that the married man with no dependents and an income of $2,500 in 1942, by reason of the doubling in the average weekly wage is today enjoying an income of $5,000, he has left over in 1954 on his $5,000 income after 1954 taxes the sum of $4,430.
The point I wish to emphasize is that while this was introduced to our income tax structure in 1942 to relieve hardship, it was not intended to be a universal deduction for everyone. Indeed, as I say, it was designed to relieve hardship, and was not intended to create benefit, unless there was more than average medical expense.
Income Tax Act
This I think was enunciated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last year when he spoke on a similar motion. I should like to quote from page 901 of Hansard for January 12, 1953, where the Minister of Finance expressed views on the principle of the measure. He said:
I think it is unsound, in principle, that normal living expenses of the individual should be paid out of income before tax.
Then he said:
If one taxpayer gets a concession or a deduction, then some other taxpayer must provide those moneys.
And again:
The philosophy behind this actually is that it is quite within the capacity of the ordinary individual to pay the normal expenses incurred for medical care or attention, but when those exceed what can be considered as a normal amount then, and then only, should there be special relief. That is the principle which lies behind the law as it stands now.
And he said further at that time, prior to the introduction some weeks later of very substantial tax relief in his budget speech:
It certainly can be argued that more equitable and widespread tax relief can be afforded in other ways.
When we are considering the equity of the floor of 3 per cent I think it is of interest to consider the similar provisions in other countries, notably in the United States. In that country the floor with respect to medical expenses still remains at 5 per cent, although hon. members are aware that while our floor was 5 per cent in 1942 it has been subject to two reductions, first to 4 per cent in 1944 and now to 3 per cent. That, I think, is an interesting development. While this was introduced in 1942 without any pressure from the opposition, or any suggestions from them, the provision has been steadily liberalized in the manner I have indicated, through reductions in the floor from 5 per cent to 4 per cent and then to 3 per cent.
Also the eligible list of medical expenses allowable under the act has been widened, and now includes insulin, ACTH, liver extract, wheel chairs, hearing aids, artificial limbs, as mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and some other items.

speechtext: Also cortisone.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Yes, cortisone. Then, in addition to that, there was a very important measure a couple of years ago which provided that bills that would be considered for income tax deductions could be those paid any time within a period of 24 months less one

Income Tax Act
day. That of course is a very important advantage to the taxpayer in the matter of the consolidation of his medical accounts during that time.
In addition to that there have been very substantial increases in the ceiling referred to by the sponsor of the motion. In 1942 the maximum amount that could be claimed by a single man as a deduction for medical expenses was $400, and for a married man $600, plus $100 for each child up to a maximum of four children. Today, with two or three revisions and greater generosity in the matter of those ceilings, these deductions stand at $1,000 for a single man or $2,000 for a married taxpayer plus $500 for each child, to a maximum of four children.
One can thus see the improvements made here. In another year subsequent to the original statute it has been made possible for a crippled or blind person to claim the expense of an attendant, to the extent of $500 or, alternatively, a blind or crippled person is given a special allowance of $500.
Other forms of concessions to taxpayers have also been provided in this relatively short space of time. Claims against an estate can now be allowed. Medical expenses incurred outside of Canada can be allowed.
Some reference has been made in the debate this afternoon by both the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) to "the little man", what the hon. member for Greenwood called the man in the low income group. I think an examination of the actual dollars and cents involved as far as the taxpayer in the low income group is concerned will show that newspaper comment concerning the advantage of this proposal has been rather exaggerated. I should like to give a few illustrations of just what it means to people in the low income groups if this motion is carried.
A single taxpayer with no dependents with an income of $1,100 would pay a tax of $17 on the 1954 tax rates. The maximum amount of saving obtained for that individual by the removal of this 3 per cent floor would be $5.61. While I am quite positive that this amount would not be without consequence to that particular taxpayer-I am not minimizing that-I think I could emphasize that that surely would not be the difference to that taxpayer between hardship and well-being.
As another example let me take a married taxpayer with no dependents who is just on the borderline of paying taxes with an income of $2,100. The maximum tax saving obtained by that taxpayer through the

proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would be $10.71. A married taxpayer with no dependents having an income of $10,000 would pay an ineome tax of $1,660 on the 1954 tax rates. With the 3 per cent floor in existence only medical expenses in excess of $300 could be deductible by that taxpayer and the result would be that $78 would be the maximum tax saved by removing the floor. I question whether in any of those instances the removal of the floor would be, as I said before, the difference between hardship and well-being.
We will look at it another way and consider the situation of a married taxpayer with two dependent children under 16 years of age who are in receipt of the family allowance. Supposing this taxpayer has an income of $3,000. The maximum saving provided by this motion would be $15.31. Let us translate that as a percentage of his total income and we find it is just about one-half of one per cent.
I do not want to overemphasize some of the problems that would be faced were this proposal accepted, but one problem is that of administration. All hon. members will realize that any deductions from gross income have to be certificated and carefully examined by officials of the Department of National Revenue. I think hon. members will readily appreciate the almost endless stream of small accounts that would be submitted for examination were all expenses allowed as deductions from income as has been proposed this afternoon.
I think hon. members could easily translate that into administrative cost and appreciate the heavy additional salary costs that would follow compared to the relatively small financial relief which I have indicated would be possible, particularly in the case of the low income group.
Let me illustrate that. As is known, a great number of persons, in the low income tax group particularly, pay their taxes by means of deductions at the source. An employer cannot anticipate what a man's medical expenses are going to be for the year and the tax deduction at the source is therefore made according to the gross income and the normal personal exemptions. It can be imagined, particularly in the case of the low income tax group which several hon. members have been emphasizing this afternoon, what administrative work would be required. Vouchers would have to be submitted and a complete check would be required because almost everybody would be putting in a claim for some rather small medical or drug expenses.

Something has been said about the revenue implications. I have had discussions with officials of the department as to what might be the loss of revenue were this proposal to be accepted. Having had some knowledge of the extensive debates that have taken place in previous years on this question I was quite prepared to give some explanation of how the officials of the department arrived at their estimate, but I do not think that is necessary this afternoon because practically all hon. members of the opposition who have referred to the loss of revenue have come quite close to the figures that our officials indicated to me would be the probable revenue lost, namely something in the neighbourhood of $35 million as a minimum. If we were to think that every taxpayer would be claiming the 3 per cent, on the basis of income subject to taxation last year that would raise the figure to probably $75 million. As I say, hon. members of the opposition more or less all admitted a revenue loss of some $35 million would be involved.
It goes without saying that if there is a loss of revenue it has to be made up in some other way. I remind the house that $35 million is greater than the surplus shown in the public accounts which were tabled here last week for the year ending March, 1953. This is given as some $23 million.
Some reference was made, particularly by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), to insurance against the hazard of medical expense, hospitalization and so on. It is true that in recent years there has been a most conspicuous growth in the number of persons who have availed themselves of the opportunity of insurance in these various forms. Hon. members will recognize that as insurance coverage increases the risk of extraordinary hazard and hardship is more or less eliminated for the insured, and thus the problem is a diminishing one.
I need only remind hon. members of the great growth of such schemes as the Blue Cross and the provision for fringe benefits in union contracts, sometimes provided by the employer and sometimes by the union. These were referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. We know also that in British Columbia and Saskatchewan there is a form of state health insurance. Then there are a great number of people who are the responsibility of the state. I refer to those in the welfare class who either through the municipality or the provinces have their medical expenses borne by the state because of lack of income.
I should like to indicate how rapid this trend has been toward insuring against the hazards of medical expenses. My source of
Income Tax Act
information is an article in the Financial Post in November 1953. This article states that the benefits paid by private accident and sickness companies in 1940 amounted to $4-3 million, and that in the short period up to 1952 those benefits had risen to $50-3 million. I am told that the benefits paid in 1945 by the Ontario Blue Cross were $1-9 million. Seven years later they were $18-8 million. One can therefore see that this problem is diminishing as people insure themselves against any extraordinary financial embarrassment as a result of sickness.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South complained that the premiums paid to insure against this form of risk were not deductible under our Income Tax Act law. That is true. But on the other hand the actual amounts paid by that individual, even though insured, if in excess of 3 per cent of his income can be submitted for income tax deduction.

That is the implication when more emphasis than "give consideration" is expected by the opposition in moving what they describe as an "abstract motion".
I suggest to members of the house that all of us have a great admiration for our British form of government. I think some of us are not envious at all of some other constitutions. Some of these as we know do not make for very stable government. Under some other forms of government close by, as we know, there seems to be a constant tug of war between the executive and legislature. Someone said this afternoon that it is a poor indication of true democracy if we were not free at this stage to vote on a principle of this kind because it involves some $35 million.

I know he would continue to make that assertion. I think you will agree that he would do so properly, having just concluded, prior to Christmas, an examination of expenditure proposals of the various departments and now being faced with responsibility to raise revenues to meet their total. consideration to tax relief amounting to some $35 million, a sum which exceeds the actual surplus of last year.
