Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have listened with interest to the remarks, made by the only member, except the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), who has spoken for the government on this resolution. I refer to the attempt made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance to persuade the house to turn down this motion. I gather, in view of the stand he has taken, and in view of the fact that apparently the government has decided not to move the adjournment of the debate as it did last year but rather to let the matter come to a vote, that it will be a bit of a surprise if we are as successful today as we were in 1952.
Before I proceed to reply to some of the remarks made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, I wish to express my thanks to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and to my colleagues, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), for the vocal support they have given to this resolution. I was sorry that the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry), the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais), and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), who spoke in support of this resolution when it had government favour two years ago, did not get to their feet today.
The arguments put forward by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance are to a large extent the same arguments that have been put forward upon previous occasions, and I suppose someone over there

Income Tax Act
will say that my replies will be the same replies. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, in view of the kind of arguments that are being advanced against the fairness of my proposal I feel that I should say a word about some of these arguments.
One of the first arguments put forward by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance was that the exemption levels in relation to the income tax were a lot lower in 1942 when this medical expense deduction provision was first written into the Income Tax Act than are the corresponding income tax exemption levels now. In my view the parliamentary assistant answered his own argument when he admitted that there has been a considerable increase in the cost of living as well as in the rates of incomes of our people since 1942. Actually in my view, if we are going to be fair, the exemption levels should have been raised a great deal more than they have been raised, bearing in mind what they were in 1942 and what they are now.
In any event, whether or not we agree on the point to which these exemption levels were raised, I suggest that they are related to the general cost of living and that they have no bearing whatsoever on other principles of income tax legislation. The fact that these exemption levels have changed has not altered the provision with respect to the deductibility of charitable donations. Why should that change have any bearing on the question of medical expenses? It has not altered the provision with respect to all the various deductible items that are allowed to business. They are still carried along despite the fact that there have been these increases in the exemption levels.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, in another part of his argument, also referred to the tremendous difference in the rates of taxation in 1942 as compared with today. There was quite a difference in the cost of government in 1942 as compared with today, particularly because of the fact that we were in the midst of a very real war, back in 1942. The rates of taxation were much higher for that reason, and the country accepted those higher rates because they were necessary for the purposes of the war.
The parliamentary assistant makes a great deal out of the fact that Mr. Ilsley described his introduction of this proposal as being made on the basis of medical expenses being a hardship to the ordinary taxpayer, a hardship in view of the larger amount of the taxpayer's income that was being siphoned off by the income tax. Again I do not want to

put a silly idea into the head of the parliamentary assistant or the minister, but if he is going to use the argument that this provision was only put in because of the hardship of excessive medical expenses in the light of excessive wartime taxation, then you would think he would remove the deductible aspect of medical expenses altogether once that so-called element of hardship has been removed. The reason he has not done so, I think, is that society has moved along and there has been substituted for that reason Mr. Ilsley gave in 1942 the recognition by society today of the importance of income tax legislation giving some recognition to medical expenses.
Another argument used by the parliamentary assistant was that the amount that would be saved by the ordinary taxpayers, particularly those in the lower brackets, would not be very great. I was a little surprised at the manner in which he put those figures forward. He seemed to act as though he were giving the house something that would be strange, figures that would make me uncomfortable from my point of view. He used illustrations in the very brackets I used in my earlier speech. As a matter of fact he came out with figures not greatly different from some of the figures about which I was complaining.
Following that line of argument the parliamentary assistant said that in the case of a couple with two children whose income was $3,000, the maximum possible saving as a result of removing the 3 per cent floor would be only $15.30 per year. I believe that is a mark of the attitude of this government. They do not seem to realize what $15.30 means to a family man with two children and $250 per month when that family is faced with heavy medical expenses. To the parliamentary assistant, the Minister of Finance or the government, $15.30 may be just peanuts, but every nickel is a help to a family faced with medical expenses. Similarly, he suggested that a single person with an income of $1,100 would be faced with a maximum saving of $5.61 per year as a result of passing my motion. The implication the parliamentary assistant put forward was that it was not worth passing this resolution for such a small saving per year.
The other day a bill was presented which was supposed to be all right because it would take only a few cents or a few dollars from the people in the course of a year. I cannot mention the bill because it is not before us now, but everybody knows what I mean. I suggest that here again you have a mark

of the attitude of this government. They do not realize what every dollar means to a person who is hit by medical expenses.

May I point out that any sum a wealthy person is likely to be able to deduct if he spends a great deal of money on medical expenses is not likely to be changed by the 3 per cent floor, because if he spends a great deal of money he is caught at the other end as well, namely by the ceiling. So far as I am concerned, the removal of the floor would not alter his position but would be of real help to the little fellow. I remind hon. members again of what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) said in an earlier debate, that the removal of the floor would help the fellow who is just over the line. It is on behalf of that group in our society that I urge this resolution be passed by this house.
Another of the arguments put forward by the parliamentary assistant was that the removal of the floor would mean additional administrative tasks for the Department of National Revenue. He says, for example, that the 3 per cent floor means that a great many people do not make deductions for medical expenses. They do not put in the receipts 83276-771
Income Tax Act
they get from doctors and hospitals because the amounts do not add up to a figure equal to 3 per cent of their gross income. Surely that is no argument against doing something that is fair in principle. The government permits deductions for charitable donations from the first dollar, which encourages the taxpayer with a receipt for even one donation to charity to claim that deduction. I suggest that the argument on an administrative basis hardly holds water.
As I am going along it occurs to me that it should be clear in all of this discussion that the 3 per cent floor does not relate to the taxable income of the taxpayer. It does not relate to his income after he has deducted the $1,000 in the case of a single person or the $2,000 in the case of a married person. For all practical purposes the 3 per cent floor is related to his gross income. There are one or two things like trade union dues or donations to approved pension plans that can be deducted before applying the 3 per cent floor, but that is all. For all practical purposes this 3 per cent floor relates to the gross income, not to the taxable income. This point has been recognized by no less a body than the chamber of commerce in the city from which the Minister of National Health and Welfare comes, the Windsor chamber of commerce. I am sure he must be interested in what they have to say.
The Windsor chamber of commerce argues that if the government cannot go all the way in what we are asking for, at least they should relate the floor to the taxable income of the taxpayer rather than to his gross income. I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will give some consideration to that compromise point of view suggested by the chamber of commerce of his own city.
The next point to which the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance referred -and he did it quickly; I gathered that he had figures he was ready to use if we challenged the amount seriously-was in respect to the amount that would be lost by reason of taking off this floor of 3 per cent. But since, at least for the purposes of the debate, we accepted the government's figure that the loss might be of the order of $30 million, he did not go into the matter extensively.
I was interested, however, in his comments at that point. They were so typical of government comment, and they were made right in the face of an alternative suggestion made in this debate by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Maedonnell). The hon. member for Greenwood pointed out that this $30 million would be only one sixty-fifth of the

Income Tax Act
amount we are spending on defence, and that conceivably it might be made up by economies in that department of government to the extent of one sixty-fifth.
But no; so far as the government is concerned, whenever we suggest tax relief that might mean a slight reduction in revenue, it never seems to think this might be made up by some form of economy. No; they always say that the only way to make it up is by getting revenue from some other source.
I said in my earlier remarks that if it had to be obtained from some source, well and good. In our view it could be obtained in a fairer way. But I challenge the government not only to think in terms of turning to another source, but rather to think in terms of the possibility of economies to make possible this very fair proposal of removing the 3 per cent floor.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion is one that, to say the least, is innocuous in its import as I see it. Although there is no reason whatever for any strong opposition to it, it does not meet the problem faced by the wheat board with respect to undistributed amounts on hand. I have here the wheat board report for 1950-51. It shows that for the year ended July 31, 1951, the amount due to producers on wheat, in so far as final payments were concerned, was over $9 million and on coarse grains $146,000, and that there was a balance in adjustment payments on wheat and coarse grains of approximately $2,600,000, or a total of $11,792,000. For the year 1952 the amount shown as being due to producers is approximately $5,417,000.
While on the face of it this motion can cause no serious objection to be raised, it does not really meet the problem that faces the wheat board in connection with the amount held to the credit of producers. I realize, as the hon. member has said, that many of the amounts that are held are held to the credit of estates and have not been claimed. While I feel that this resolution, if carried, will have a favourable result in so far as it purports to establish scholarships, it does not meet the problem of the disposal of the amounts on hand.
I suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that it must be a serious problem for the wheat board to have such large amounts on hand to the credit of producers whose addresses are not known and for which no claims have been made. Therefore I pass on to him a suggestion I have heard made on occasion, and no doubt it has been made to him before on many occasions, namely that the wheat board might follow a similar system to that followed by the chartered banks and from time to time advertise a list of those names to whose credit moneys are held by the wheat board. While the cost of such advertising might be considerable, I am sure many hundreds of thousands of dollars, if not millions, now unclaimed would go into the hands of the proper claimants.
One finds frequently in the practice of law, and particularly in the administration of estates, that those to whom moneys have been credited having passed away without leaving any record of having moneys to their credit, such claims are overlooked.
I feel that whether or not this motion is carried the hon. member has performed a fine function in bringing this subject before the house, because it does enable a discussion to take place as to the disposition of those funds, to the end that millions of dollars may
121G

Wheat Board-Scholarships be distributed among the proper claimants. I do not know what the latest figures are because the 1953 annual report is not available.
Some might say that there is negligence on the part of the individuals for whom these moneys are held. That is not my view at all. The position of these people is much the same as those who, having credit balances in the banks, leave the locality, pass away or somehow cease to realize that the credit is there for them. It is only through advertising that these credits become known. Certainly I got a surprise on one occasion when one of the chartered banks showed I had a balance of $10.50 on hand in one of its branches. I know I would not have realized it if publicity had not been given to the fact. I know many who have had large amounts and who have had the same experience.
So far as the disposal of the moneys is concerned, the hon. member has suggested that they be set aside to establish a scholarship fund to be awarded to the sons and daughters of prairie farmers attending universities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Generally speaking that is a very fine objective, and no one could take any serious objection to it. I do not know whether the farm organizations made the suggestion that is now placed before the house by the hon. member, or whether in making this suggestion he represents a considerable group of farmers within Saskatchewan. Certainly as a general principle there can be no objection, but if it is accepted I can see tremendous difficulties in the way of extending these benefits. I can see no reason for casting a vote against it, for at least it envisages providing some benefit from the moneys so held by the wheat board, but who is to be entitled to it? How is it to be disbursed and on what basis? All those things are merely matters of detail.
I rise to say that the motion has in it no serious objection that I can see. I feel it would be favourably received by people in general, having the objective in mind. I believe that a more serious problem faces the wheat board, and that is the need for an out and out advertising campaign setting out the moneys held for a period of at least three years in order to clear up this large amount of money that is today apparently unclaimed from the wheat board.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several observations I should make in connection with this resolution. The first relates to the amount of money in the fund, and where the money would come from in the first place. I think

it is interesting to go through the Canadian wheat board report for the crop year 1951-52, which gives the history of the payments which were outstanding, beginning with the 1940 crop account.
For the 1940 crop account the present total of outstanding certificates and cheques is $86,672.01; in the 1941 crop account, $38,444.99; in the 1942 crop account, $44,447.05. Now we come to the 1943 crop account, in which there is a significant increase to $178,481.11; in the 1944 crop account another increase to $209,246.14; in the 1945-49 pool account, the total amounted to $2,013,355.52; while in the 1950-51 pool account it amounted to $683,169.99, the total for that period being $3,253,816.81. During the period from August 1, 1952 to November 30, 1952, the board paid $1,115,531.94 in respect to its liability of $3,388,375.58, leaving a total outstanding at that period of $2,272,843.64. As the hon. member has pointed out, the figure would stand now at just about $2-5 million.
Now, going back to show where the funds would come from, we see that they may be from cheques for participation payments made out to farmers who are perhaps deceased. I think the board has a responsibility to try to find those who would inherit the estate and who would have a rightful claim against those funds. There are those who have moved out of the locality. There may be retired farmers who have moved to some of the larger centres or perhaps out to the balmy breezes of British Columbia. As I understand it, these cheques are sent out by mail. If the individual to whom the cheque is directed is not available in the locality, and the postmaster does not know where he is, I presume the cheque would be returned to the Canadian wheat board. The board would assume the cheque was undeliverable. I presume the board would make several attempts to deliver it to make certain that the individual was not just absent at that particular time.
One difficult point is that an individual may be entitled to a payment, and may be living at an adjacent point. He may have delivered grain during an open quota to a point some 15 miles distant from his residence, and the postmaster at that point would not be personally acquainted with him.
I think we are safe in saying that in all cases the individuals are unaware that there is a credit standing in their name. As the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has pointed out, there should be an active campaign to inform the public

about those who are entitled to these funds. During the years I have farmed in my district not once have I seen a list of such individuals who were entitled to payments from the Canadian wheat board. I do not say that such lists do not exist, but I have never seen them. I would suggest to the minister, then, that an extensive advertising program be carried out in the newspapers in these areas, setting out the names of individuals who have credits with the Canadian wheat board.
I do not think it should be left to the individual to write to the Canadian wheat board and inquire if there is a credit there.
I notice the hon. member for Meadow Lake has put an arbitrary period of six years in his resolution, after which the funds would become available for a trust fund. It is pointed out also that further claims may be made at any time during that period. I would just question the six-year period. I think it would be more advisable to put it on a ten-year basis, since going back ten years would bring us to the 1942 crop year, where we still have a little more than $150,000 as a beginning, and we could carry on the program from there.
Assuming every possible effort has been made to locate the owners, I think the suggestion that funds be used for educational purposes is very commendable. They should be used to assist those who created them. One method suggested is that of a scholarship fund. I believe it might be well to say here that a relatively small number of the sons and daughters of farmers are able to take advantage of higher education. When I refer to "higher education" I might include high schools. Their services may be required on the farms, or they may be in isolated locations where they are unable to take advantage of high school education.
Therefore I would question the value of confining the assistance to university scholarships, which would afford an advantage to only a small segment of our agricultural population. Only a small proportion of farm personnel, or farm boys and girls, attend university. I think it is equally significant that a very small percentage of them return to the farms to impart the advantage of their knowledge to the local communities. In many instances the students follow non-agricultural lines of study. They may study to become doctors, dentists or lawyers, in which case their studies are of value to them as well as to agriculture, but not directly to the communities from which they have come. I say they are of value to agriculture because we must face the fact that, because of the 83276-78
18, 1954	1217
Wheat Board-Scholarships increase in technology, fewer people are able to farm the same amount of land. Therefore some will be forced off the farms into other lines of endeavour. Anything we can do by way of assistance for them is certainly valuable.
I think a more direct method of spending these funds would be desirable. This could take the form of direct assistance to the communities, through farm organizations. It could provide funds for educational work. I think we are all aware of the significance and value of adult education and the effect it has upon the cultural practices of the farming communities. In my view if funds were made available for local organizations so that, for example, they could organize tours to experimental farms, where the farmers could see the most up-to-date farming techniques and where they could see the development of new varieties, we would do more for agriculture than by awarding scholarships in universities.
In my constituency we are very close to two first-class experimental farms. I refer to those at Swift Current and at Scott. On more than one occasion farmers in that area have organized themselves to tour these experimental stations, and they are very enthusiastic about what they see. Upon returning to their farms they try to put into practice some of the policies they have seen demonstrated. If various farm organizations had funds available to charter buses and organize tours so the farmers in the district would have the opportunity of seeing these demonstrations which otherwise would be denied to them, it would be to their advantage.
In the field of adult education we cannot be negligent of a simple matter such as weed control. It would be advantageous if the farmers could acquaint themselves with weeds and the techniques required for their eradication. In this way the productivity of the farms would be increased.
Just as an example I would point out that some years back an individual in Kindersley received a plant known as toad flax. It looks a good deal like snapdragon. He brought it home with him and planted it in his garden, thinking it to be a pretty flower. I have no doubt many hon. members from northern Saskatchewan will be familiar with toad flax and the damage it can do to land. I might say that today there is a small patch of this weed growing on the fair grounds at Kindersley, and I am sure if the farmers in the community were aware of the dangers from this weed they would be out there tomorrow morning shovelling off the snow

Wheat Board-Scholarships and chopping out all they could find. If one goes about 150 miles north of there he can see the devastation that can be caused by such an innocent looking plant as toad flax.
Another aspect in connection with education in the rural areas with which we must concern ourselves is the desirability of encouraging boys' and girls' club work. If a local farm organization had the funds with which to sponsor such a club it would instil in the minds of boys and girls knowledge of good farming practices. They would be taught individual responsibilities, the value of good seed, the value of education and of companionship. The other 4-H clubs are of equal value; I am thinking of calf clubs, tractor clubs and others suited to the locality.
These are some aspects we must consider when the disposition of funds from the wheat board is before us. I agree with the underlying principle of the bill, that the funds should be utilized after every effort has been made to locate the owners. They should be used to provide assistance through scholarships and assistance to the local community. However, as the resolution is now worded it does not allow for assistance to the community, and I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden):
That the resolution be amended by inserting therein immediately after the words "earnings thereon" in the third last line, the following:
" (a) partly";
and by adding at the end of the said resolution the following:
"and (b) partly as a fund to be paid to bona fide farm organizations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the British Columbia block, for use in educational work among their own membership and other primary producers in those areas."
With this amendment the resolution would read;
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act to provide that, where producers of any grain sold or delivered during a pool period have been for six years or more entitled to receive from the board payments in respect thereof under certificates issued pursuant to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, or out of an equalization fund, and there is an undistributed balance remaining in the accounts of the board in respect of that grain, such undistributed balances be paid over to trustees who shall be instructed to pay claims as they are submitted, to invest the remainder in appropriate government securities, and to set aside the interest earnings thereon (a) partly as a scholarship fund to be awarded to the sons and daughters of prairie farmers attending the universities of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and (b) partly as a fund to be paid to bona fide farm organizations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the British Columbia block, for use in educational work among their own membership and other primary producers in those areas.
These funds should be more widely advertised so that farmers would become aware
[Mr. Johnson (Kindersley) .1
of them and would have an opportunity to make their claims. I should like to see the resolution carried in the form I have suggested, so that something would be done to provide financial assistance to bona fide farm organizations to provide for adult education and assistance for boys' and girls' club work.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must admit frankly that I have not given this matter a great deal of thought, but on the face of it I would support the general principle contained in the resolution, that after a certain period of time unclaimed balances held by the wheat board should be turned over to a board of trustees. This board would meet any claims made by farmers who were eligible to receive payment and the balance would be invested, the interest thereon being used for the purpose of providing scholarships for daughters and sons of farmers.
The first question that comes to my mind is whether this matter has been discussed with the various farm organizations, and what is their reaction to the suggestion. Surely if we are going to go ahead with a proposal of this kind farm organizations in the west should be consulted. They might be able to offer many suggestions with regard to this matter. It seems strange to me that we should go ahead with a motion of this kind without first getting their advice. If I remember rightly they did make some suggestions regarding the utilization of these funds in the past, but I forget just what it was. I do know that at the time I was not quite in accord with the suggestions they did make.
Another point that comes to my mind is in connection with the suggested period of six years. In view of the fact that the vast majority of payments are completed in about three years I wonder if it would be necessary to wait six years. The hon. member who preceded me suggested ten years, but I would go in the opposite direction and suggest that if at the end of three years every effort to find the owners of unclaimed moneys had been without success, then it should be paid over to the board of trustees. Those trustees would still be able to pay any claims that were made, and in the meantime the money could be invested and put to useful purposes.
When I say "useful purposes" I do not suppose that the money is actually lying idle. Perhaps the wheat board borrows it to pay operating expenses. I am not certain as to that, but I suppose there is nothing to stop the wheat board borrowing the money and using it to pay operating expenses and thus saving the interest they would have

to pay if the money were borrowed from a chartered bank. Perhaps that is a point the hon. member would clarify if he replies.
I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) that greater efforts should be made to locate the owners of this money by advertising. I have never seen printed in a newspaper any list of names of people to whom balances are owing. If the names of farmers in each of the provinces were printed in some of the principal papers, even though the actual farmer who was entitled to receive payment did not see it some of his friends might, and perhaps they would know where the farmer was living and notify him that he had money coming to him. In that way it might be possible to get more of these unpaid balances paid directly to the farmers.
The amendment suggests that a certain amount of this money should be paid to farm organizations to be utilized for a number of community purposes. The danger in that suggestion is that the money might be spread too far and too thin, with the result that not much could be done for anybody. No doubt there is enough money at the present time to provide scholarships on quite a substantial scale if it were invested, but if you tried to use the money for many different purposes you might find you were unable to accomplish anything worth while.
Another point is what farm organizations would be eligible to receive this money. I imagine that the minute you start talking about making money available you will have requests from many bodies. There would be the Canadian Federation of Agriculture; there would be the three western farm unions, the wheat pools, the western livestock growers' association, the grain growers' association. I do not know just where you would stop making contributions to various organizations.
Personally if action of this kind is going to be taken I would prefer to support the resolution as it stands, with perhaps a change in the period of six years to three years. I do not see why we should hold the money for that length of time. The three-year period would permit the wheat board to try to get in touch with farmers by means of advertising.
On those conditions we will be quite prepared to support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution is one on which I think it would be helpful to have the views of a number of hon. members. The resolution 83276-78J
Wheat Board-Scholarships suggests an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I would point out that a similar resolution appeared on the order paper last session, moved by the then hon. member for Mackenzie, Mr. Ferrie. If I am not mistaken the wording was identical. The resolution was not reached or discussed as a resolution during that session, but I looked on it with a good deal of favour. As a matter of fact I helped Mr. Ferrie draft it, or at least suggested the wording.
During that session we did amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act and in doing so we made provision for an arrangement somewhat similar to that suggested by this resolution. We provided that after funds had been outstanding for six years they would be segregated in a separate account which could be used as determined by the governor in council on the recommendation of the wheat board. The first intention had been to be more specific and carry out the terms of the resolution in full. However, on consulting the farm organizations it was found that there were as many different ideas about how the fund should be used as there were farm organizations.
Since we could not at that time determine a policy which would be satisfactory to the representatives of the farmers, we decided that we would simply allocate the money in a fund and allow some time for the wheat board to work out a solution that would be reasonably satisfactory to those who speak with some authority for the western producers.
I think the amount of money involved is being somewhat exaggerated. After setting aside all outstanding balances that were six years old, that is six years from the date on which the payment was due, the amount that accrued to the fund totalled $458,344.37. Perhaps I should read this paragraph from what I said at that time, and I quote from page 3425 of Hansard of March 30, 1953:
Every effort has been made to locate the persons to whom this money is due. Advertisements have been used. Letters have been sent. The help of the wheat pool organizations has been requisitioned to try to trace them down. The balances that it is proposed to set aside at the moment are those from the 1940 crop wheat account, the 1941 crop, the 1942 crop and the 1943 crop. To support the general proposal advanced by my colleague the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson) I should like to say that I believe that adult education will require a good deal of financial assistance. The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) cannot hope to suggest this proposal as a substitute for federal aid for education. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out, the sum is not going to be large. The balance he mentioned, namely $458,000 invested at 3 per cent, would give something less than $14,000 per year. If that amount were to be divided among the three prairie provinces, none would get a large amount.
I would suggest that the amount spent on university education should be earmarked for research for specific work. I think no useful purpose would be served if a student went to university and later went to California, New York city or Washington. I suggest that for every year of tuition a student accepted from the fund, one year at
Wheat Board-Scholarships least should be spent on research work in. the area where he lives or where he studies, with a view to solving some of the problems that I should like to submit for the consideration of the house.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, for example, in its December bulletin sets out the position of the farmer in August, 1953, as compared with the position in August, 1949. It shows the position to be as follows:
Taxes, increase 16-4 per cent; Farm wages, increase 22-6 per cent; Farm machinery, increase 25 per cent; Building materials, increase 31 per cent; Gas, oil, etc., increase 10 per cent; Feed, decrease -6 per cent; Fertilizer, increase 28-8 per cent; Seed, decrease 5 per cent; Farm family living costs, increase 17 per cent.
With those drastic increases in farm operating costs, on the next page we find this statement:
Figuring 1949 as a basis of 100, the purchasing power of net farm income in 1953 works out at 90.
While everyone dealing in farm machinery, building materials, fertilizer and feed is able to pass on the increase to the consumer, the farmer is in the unfortunate position that his net position is worse in 1953 than it was in 1949.
In one of the other federation bulletins it is indicated that a great deal of educational work should be done in all parts of Canada in order to help people to get a little bit better sense of values. Here is what is stated:
Let's take the year 1950. In this year the people of Canada spent a total of $1 billion on tobacco and alcoholic beverages. We could compare this with the total value of the wheat crop of that year at $712 million, or the total value of all cereal crops of 1950, including wheat, oats, barley, rye, at $1-2 billion. Or we could compare it with the total value of milk production at $432 million.
That is in contrast with a thousand millions of dollars spent on tobacco and alcoholic beverages. I submit that here would be a field for a university student to do graduate work, with a view to helping the people of Canada get a better sense of values, so that agriculture might get a larger share of the consumers' dollars. In 1952 our people spent $1,243 million on tobacco and alcoholic beverages, and on milk they spent $360 million. We find our expenditure on milk going down and our expenditure on alcoholic beverages and tobacco going up. I think all the people in the prairie provinces who have contributed to this fund that we are discussing tonight would agree that here is a field for some work by some students in some of the universities in western Canada.
The editor of the Western Producer had something to say in an editorial entitled

In it he pointed out that in the United States for 1954 the program for agriculture calls for reducing drastically the level of support prices, thus discouraging production and also enforcing a substantial cut in acreage sown to crops in surplus. The comment is this:
Here we have a situation which should give pause not only to the Americans but to the whole free world. For surely it affords the most disturbing and distressing proof of the complete bankruptcy of our economic system.
It points out that the crying need of the world is for food, and goes on to say:
It would be wearisome repetition to quote the pronouncements of the food and agriculture organization and other authorities, showing that more than half of the people on the outside of the iron curtain are always hungry-never get a decent meal. On the radio every day our hearts are wrung by appeals for donations of scraps of food to feed the starving. At the same time the farmers of the United States have demonstrated what they and farmers elsewhere can do when given adequate stimulus. They can produce food in such abundance that it becomes a problem to find storage space for it. Then what happens? Well, we see it actually happening right now in the United States. Instead of welcoming the abundance as a God-given respite for the starving multitudes, a frantic effort is made to cut back production. We have the food and there is more where it came from but how to get it to those who need it-that's the problem that stumps the experts. So, may God forgive us, we are proposing to solve the problem of abundance by reducing production, thus creating an artificial scarcity. What more devastating indictment of our economic system could even its most fanatical critic conceive?
That is in the United States. But in Canada not so long ago we took our part in keeping down production. The editorial continues:
It would be a tragic mistake to run away with the idea that these matters interest only one country or affect only the farmers, that the problem is not of major proportions, and, anyway, is only temporary. In plain truth it is one of the principal symptoms of the disease that is killing civilization. For if civilization should perish and freedom die it will be because of the rot within it. The average man does not take fire from eloquent exhortations that it is his duty to defend "our way of life" with his own life if necessary. Wrongly, no doubt, having enjoyed free institutions all his life he takes them for granted like the air he breathes. He judges the value of "our way of life" by its economic performance and because he has himself, in so many instances, experienced the corroding effects of poverty in the midst of plenty, he judges that it has been a miserable failure.

Over half the people in the world are illiterate, thus providing fertile soil for the weeds and tares of superstition, prejudice and fanaticism. Mr. Speaker, the minister has stated that the real purpose of this resolution can be served by hearing from hon. members as to ways in which this money might be spent. I suggest to the minister that there is another purpose in the resolution which is quite important, too. In section 5 of the act amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act passed last year we find the following:
Any balance transferred to the separate account pursuant to subparagraph (it) of paragraph (a) of
Wheat Board-Scholarships subsection 1 shall be used for such purposes as the governor in council, upon the recommendation of the board, may deem to be for the benefit of producers.
In other words the governor in council has to appropriate the money on the recommendation of the wheat board. I suggest for the consideration of the minister that the wheat board is very busy with the problems involved in the marketing of wheat, and that it is going outside its own field when you ask it to try to decide in what way this money could be spent in the best interests of producers. It might have to decide between competing claims for this money, and the board might not want to do that in view of the fact that it is supposed to serve producers with respect to marketing their grain. It might not want to adjudicate between conflicting claims.
I suggest that the resolution should be considered by the government from the standpoint of the proposed setting up of a board to advise the governor in council as to the use of this money, and that in view of the fact it is going to spend money which belongs essentially to the producers of western Canada such a board should be very closely in touch with what might be considered in the best interests of the producers of western Canada. The personnel of such a board might consist, for example, of the presidents of western universities or the deans of agriculture of the western universities. If such a board were constituted it would doubtless come forward in a very short time with some suggestion to the government as to how this money might be used to the best advantage of the producers of western Canada.
The difficulty with the present legislation is that the wheat board is so busy with its normal work that it does not have the time, is not set up to investigate and would not want to weigh competing claims. I suggest, whether this resolution carries or is withdrawn, that the government should consider amending the legislation to put the matter of recommendation as to how this money should be used in the hands of a board of trustees constituted perhaps of the heads of the western universities or the deans of agriculture of the western universities. If the matter is placed in their hands there are so many worth-while matters that would be helpful to western agriculture about which they would know that there would be no delay in coming forward with suggestions as to ways in which this money might be used.

Wheat Board-Scholarships
I think that is what the mover of the motion had in mind when he spoke about using this money for scholarships to be awarded to the sons and daughters of prairie farmers attending the universities of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. I fancy that not only would he have in mind assisting the children of prairie farmers as such, but in addition that the work they might do would also be furthering the best interests of the farmers of western Canada. It is for that reason I suggest that this board should be composed of the deans of agriculture of the western universities, because in awarding these scholarships they would have in mind the people who would be likely to carry on for western agriculture. The proposed scholarships probably would be postgraduate research scholarships to enable research to be carried on in some field that needed work done in it, and for which there was not the necessary money.
I do, therefore, heartily commend the hon. member for Meadow Lake for moving this resolution. If we are going to have steps taken without delay to make use of these moneys, we need to put the matter into the hands of a special board set up for the purpose, and leave that board to deal with the way in which this money might be used. I would think the wheat board would be pleased to be relieved of this duty that is placed upon it by last year's amendment. I suggest that the government give consideration to further amending the wheat board act to provide for advice by this board, to be set up somewhat along the line I have mentioned. It seems to me that a board such as that would be better able to decide how best to use this money than we sitting here and making decisions more or less offhand.

Mr. Speaker, the only reason that prompts me to take part in this discussion is a fact which has been mentioned by many of the people who have spoken, that the subject is of interest to western farmers. Therefore I should like to say a few words in support of the principle involved. I heartily agree with the proposed disposition of this money.
Someone suggested that possibly it could be used to better advantage by educating the rest of the people of Canada as to the farmers' problems. I feel, however, that possibly the resolution does not go quite far enough. I have thought that possibly we could go a little farther with it. In view of the remarks by the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few minutes ago in that regard, that does not seem to be the case. I should like to read the resolution as proposed by the farm union

of Alberta; the British Columbia bloc; the Saskatchewan farmers' union; the Manitoba farmers' union, and the Ontario farmers' union in their submission to the Canadian wheat board. They say:
We would recommend, after moneys have been unclaimed In the Canadian wheat board funds for a period of six years that a special trust account be set up under a board of trustees approved by the farmers, that a portion of these moneys and the annual interest accrued thereon be made available to the three farm unions periodically on a basis of and in proportion to the amount of deliveries of grain during these years from each province.
This again brings up the fact that there are a great many farm organizations in western Canada which would undoubtedly lay claim to this money. I was a little disappointed on learning that the amount involved was not as great as some of us had been led to believe. I believe there are some 14 different farm organizations in western Canada which undoubtedly would lay claim to a part of this money. Nevertheless the idea is good, and it is something that has been proposed by other branches of agriculture. For instance, the stock organizations have been proposing that the horned cattle fund be turned over to the universities to carry on work in connection with livestock.
A year ago I had an opportunity of discussing this subject with Dr. Bell of the University of Saskatchewan who, incidentally, is Canada's outstanding man in the field of animal nutrition. He was deploring the fact that trained personnel were not available in the field of animal nutrition to carry out very important work which needed to be done. He also deplored the fact that facilities for carrying out the work were inadequate, and much time had to be consumed in carrying out particular research. It was felt that this did not apply only to universities in Saskatchewan but to many universities with which Dr. Bell had been acquainted. I know it can be argued that the money is being used to the advantage of farmers now. However, I feel that it could be used to even greater advantage. I had hoped that possibly we would have access to some of the principal in the hands of the wheat board, but as I said a moment ago the minister indicated that was not to be had.
I am sorry I cannot go along with the hon. member for Kindersley and support what he said about the lists of names of men who had money in this fund in order to locate them. I know that at my grain delivery point in Tisdale I have often seen lists of names of men who had money in this particular fund. When I heard the hon. member for Kindersley I thought possibly what I

had seen was not a directive from the wheat board, but the minister said a moment ago that the board had received co-operation in posting these names. I presume, therefore, there is some neglect on the part of local elevator agencies when these names are not posted.
However, I should like to add that possibly these names should be listed once a year in the local farm newspapers in order to do everything possible to see that these men are notified they have money in the fund. I believe there are a great many retired farmers who would be quite anxious to give that money to a scholarship that might further the aims of the agriculturists in western Canada. I believe that is a possibility that has some merit.
A moment ago I mentioned that no decision has yet been made about what to do with the horned cattle fund. I imagine that it will be turned over to this work, regardless of how small the fund may be. As the hon. member for Mackenzie stated, a fund of $14,000 or $15,000 would help. We are in hopes that it will be more than that, but even that amount could be used to great advantage.
I should like to mention just one phase of research work which is carried on in the University of Saskatchewan which could use money if it were made available in this way. I am thinking of the work done in connection with rhinitis, a disease of swine. I was out to the experimental farm in Ottawa recently in connection with research that is going on at the farm at Lacombe. Today there is absolutely no clue to a possible solution to this problem. In talking to Dr. Bell I was convinced that the solution will not be found until they have more trained personnel who are prepared to take on some of the more technical work.
I must go along with the hon. member for Kindersley, who has said that practical farm problems could be attacked if some of this money were made available. I might point out that a royal commission has been set up in Saskatchewan to deal with rural life. I am sure that before many months we are going to see that the position of the farmers in western Canada will have to be studied. It will require a great deal more study than can be given to it by one royal commission. Perhaps some of this money could be spent along those lines.
I think the idea in the resolution is sound, and I support the principle of it. Some move along this line has been long overdue, and I was happy to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce speak as he did in support of this
Wheat Board-Scholarships plan. I do not think I can add anything more at the moment. I think all hon. members are agreed that the principle is sound. In spite of what has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the hon. member for Meadow Lake who sponsors the resolution, I still feel the amendment has merit, and I shall support it.

Mr. Speaker, no one I am sure will disagree with this resolution, dealing as it does with the problem of education in the rural parts of the prairies. It does make a small contribution to the subject of education in those areas. In our prairie provinces we are faced with many educational problems, the most important of which is the fact that only a small percentage of the rural young people take advantage of the opportunities offered in higher education.
The resolution would seem to offer some assistance in this direction, in giving encouragement by way of scholarships to the group of young people eligible to take advantage of higher education. Before coming to the house it was my opportunity to be in touch annually with most of the high schools in the western part of Manitoba, as well as southeastern Saskatchewan. I found that notwithstanding the increased enrolments in our universities and colleges since the war, it is still true that there are some rural communities that never send any of their high school graduates to institutions of higher learning, chiefly because the tradition of the pursuit of higher learning has not yet been generally established in the rural parts of the prairies.
I do not know the statistics for the provinces outside Manitoba, but I do know that some two years ago statistics for registrations at the University of Manitoba, as between rural and urban students, stood at a ratio of something like 75 per cent urban and 25 per cent rural. I am sure the same pattern would be established in the other prairie provinces.
Going a little further in this matter the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that the key problem in connection with the resolution was to decide how the money could best be disbursed for educational purposes. I would suggest that two critical problems in the rural west are those of entrance scholarships and the great need for encouraging research activities.
In connection with entrance scholarships, I am sure there are many eligible young people, so far as academic standards are concerned, who would carry on their studies in our institutions of higher learning, if the necessary financial stimulus was provided to

Wheat Board-Scholarships
get them over the initial hurdle. Even though on the prairies tuition fees and general living expenses at our colleges and universities may not be as high as they are in the eastern part of Canada, it is still true, unfortunately, that the expense of higher education is sufficiently great to discourage many students who have demonstrated high academic ability in their high school education.
I am one who believes that any student who fits into that rare category of exceptional academic ability should have the opportunity to carry on his or her educational interests in a chosen field. There are many scholarship schemes already available in our prairie universities and colleges, but I do not think the demand could ever be exhausted. When we consider the relatively small sum that would be available from the fund mentioned in the resolution-I believe it amounts to $14,000 a year-I am sure there would be no difficulty whatsoever in apportioning the amount equitably among the three prairie provinces.
Therefore I would strongly recommend that in addition to setting aside part of this fund for research purposes, consideration be given to making some of it available for entrance scholarships. I would not leave the matter at the entrance level, because I know from personal experience that we have students who succeed in meeting the necessary costs in the first year of higher education, only to find it necessary at that time to withdraw. I suggest that any student who in his first year at university has demonstrated exceptional ability should be permitted to draw on the fund to assist in the continuation of his studies, if financial need demands such action.
I do not need to stress the great necessity for research. That has already been dealt with by several hon. members. In view of the relatively small amount involved, however, I suggest it might be wise to restrict the use of these moneys to agricultural research. The surplus funds result from wheat-producing activities, and it seems only reasonable to me that such money should be used, so far as research work is concerned, to deal with problems most closely related to the agricultural field.
Since world war II many veterans from western Canada have used their re-establishment credits to train for specialized agricultural research. I have friends who otherwise would not have gone beyond high school, who have taken their doctorates in agricultural research. Many of them are now becoming active in this important field. But these funds are drying up, and it might

well be that as money becomes available through the surplus wheat board fund it could be used to fill the gap left with the completion of the D.V.A. rehabilitation program.
Turning now to the amendment, I have noticed that many hon. members who have spoken for the group that has brought forward this amendment, discovering the relative smallness of the sum involved, have begun to doubt the value of the amendment, providing that the money should be distributed among the various farm organizations. If the interest from this fund would not be more than $14,000 a year, there would be little merit in such a recommendation.
As far as general educational facilities are concerned I should like to point out that the extension departments of the three prairie universities are making an extremely valuable contribution to these activities. I refer particularly to the University of Manitoba because I have a most intimate knowledge of the activities being carried on there. The University of Manitoba has within the past few years reorganized its extension activities and appointed a full-time director of adult education. During the past two or three years its activities in connection with education among the adult population have increased at an impressive rate.
I know this work has only begun. It is hoped that regional directors of adult education will be appointed and scattered throughout the province of Manitoba to make the contribution that is so necessary in all phases of adult education, which of course would include subjects of agricultural interest. In addition to all this we have our agricultural representatives who make an excellent contribution in the field of popular adult education.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicate that the necessary amendment making it possible to implement this motion had already been made to the wheat board act. In the strongest way possible I would suggest that something be done at the earliest moment to implement the recommendations being made here this evening as provided for in the wheat board act.
I believe it was the hon. member for Ros-thern (Mr. Tucker) who suggested that an advisory board be established immediately to deal with the details involved in a program of this kind. I agree heartily with that suggestion. It seems logical to me that the deans of agriculture of the respective prairie universities would be the men best qualified to deal with specific recommendations.

I have one further suggestion to make. If it ever becomes difficult to decide who should be eligible for assistance from this fund I am sure the farm organizations, especially the 4-H clubs, could assist in the process of selecting the young people who would benefit most under this worthy program.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I were offering any objection to this resolution I think perhaps it would be that no reference to British Columbia is made in it. If I were offering an amendment I would suggest that the last two lines should read:
-the sons and daughters of prairie farmers attending the universities of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
While many hon. members may not have forgotten, perhaps they have overlooked the fact that quite a substantial amount of wheat is grown in the Peace river district of British Columbia, and to no small extent in the Creston valley district in my own riding.
There is perhaps an even more important point that has been overlooked in connection with this resolution. Where are the farmers who originally were entitled to this money which is now with the wheat board? I think it is inconceivable that the majority of them are still farming, because they have been alert to the fact that money was available and perhaps would be to their credit in the records of the wheat board. It is my opinion that a large number of the producers, either young or old, have migrated to British Columbia and retired. No doubt if advertisements were run in the British Columbia papers it would be found that a large number of claims would come from that province. If they did not come from the farmers themselves, undoubtedly there would be children of those producers who should be in a position, just as much as the children of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta farmers, to benefit from the terms of this proposed resolution.
This debate has pointed out one thing that we have always feared in connection with federal domination in the field of education. In the various resolutions that have been brought forward in this house requesting federal aid for education it has been pointed out that it is impossible to give substantial aid without there being some direction. As the hon. member for Mackenzie has indicated already, the C.C.F. party would wish, if these funds were set aside and controlled by federal legislation, to have strings attached. They are going to designate where the students should go, that they should not go
Wheat Board-Scholarships to the United States or from province to province. It is just another indication of where we are going to head when we get into this particular field.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as seconder of the resolution I should like to point out that apparently the amendment is the only part that is of much value, since what is proposed by the resolution has already been provided for by an amendment to the act. All that can be done now is to have the wheat board recommend to the governor in council what should be done with the money available. The governor general in council can then be influenced by recommendations from the board and it is up to us, I suppose, to let the board know what we as members of the house feel, and the board can pass on these recommendations to the governor in council. Since the minister himself is head of the wheat board I suppose the thing is pretty well cut and dried in any event.
Our amendment asks that a portion of the money which became available through this fund should be distributed to farm organizations throughout western Canada so they can carry on educational programs within their own organizations and among their own membership to the benefit of the people generally in their area, and I do not think we can use it for a much better purpose.
The educational program outlined here is quite good, and I would support the request of the hon. member who spoke last, that some benefits be made available to those people in that part of British Columbia who made contributions to this 'fund. Certainly they should be included in the whole set-up.
With regard to farm organizations and their educational work, anyone who has followed what has been done in the west among farmers who in the past have contributed this money and to whom it really belongs would know that ever since the inception of the old united farmers of Canada and ever since the organization of the Saskatchewan wheat pool they have set aside certain funds for carrying on educational work among farmers in the rank and file of their organizations. I do not think you will find a better informed rank and file among the agricultural population in any part of Canada than among the people of the west who constantly have these matters before them and who constantly study them. These organizations can speak with one voice, can agree on matters of principle and obtain agreement on what action should be taken and then strive toward their objective.

Wheat Board-Scholarships
At the present time you have growing in western Canada one of the finest farm organizations that was ever developed, and that is the farmers' union. The Saskatchewan branch of the farmers' union held a convention in the city of Regina in December last, and they had 1,400 delegates from all parts of that province. At that convention they threshed out the problems facing western farmers and obtained the facts with regard to present and future markets, and in relation to the present Canadian surplus. They carry on research work, but they are hampered to a large extent because there are not sufficient funds available in order to study the various forms of farm organization and development; the marketing of livestock; the future needs of the world in agriculture; and what they can do to adjust their production under existing circumstances so they can meet what the world needs.
I do not think there could be a better use made of the funds that become available than in this fashion, so these organizations can be assisted in carrying on that kind of research. I am sure these groups would heartily endorse a proposal that money of this kind should be made available to them on a membership basis to carry on educational programs. After all, the welfare of Canada depends on the welfare of its people and its producers, and if these people know what the world's needs are and can adjust their production to meet the world's needs then agricultural problems and problems of surplus can be taken care of. It would ease the way for the future. You would have a better informed population, and the rank and file would know what was required.
I hope the minister will change his opinion with regard to the value of farm organizations. I do not think this money would be spread too thinly. I believe farm organizations would get together and decide where the money could be spent on the kind of research work that would be of value to them all. I think the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Saskatchewan farmers' union, the Canadian farmers' union and the farmers' union of Manitoba are all working together and making a splendid contribution to the future welfare of their people. I do not believe these people, whose money this really is, would want anything better than that a large portion of it should be used to carry on the work of research and education among the farm organizations in the west.

in this debate. I did intend to ask the hon. member from Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) a question. Perhaps I may be permitted to ask that question through you, Mr. Speaker. Was that his idea and is it his intention that British Columbia should have its share on that basis?

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my contention that there are a large number of retired prairie farmers both young and old who have contributed a large amount to this fund, and I think they should share in the fund in proportion to their contribution. That is, if there are farmers who have retired and are living in British Columbia they should not be overlooked. If that would be difficult to work out, then let it be on the basis that British Columbia farmers who have made very great contributions would be paid on a per capita basis.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a brief word on this motion and on the amendment. I think the setting up of a fund as suggested by the hon. member for Meadow Lake is a very good idea, and I want to congratulate him for having proposed this motion. I think it should be borne in mind that this is a fund that has accumulated with the wheat board and is the result entirely of the efforts of the grain producers of the three prairie provinces; that this fund by which it is suggested we create scholarships would be set up on interest accumulated on securities to be bought by the board that would be appointed to look after the fund. That fund would provide scholarships for boys and girls of farmers of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to enable them to study in the colleges of these three provinces.
Very important research work has been done in plant and cereal fields in years gone by and through that research, particularly in regard to the problem of rust, farmers in the west have saved millions of dollars. I know a young man from my constituency by the name of Leonard Shebeske who took up research work before the war and followed it up afer the war under a similar scholarship which he obtained, and through hard work he is now a professor at the Manitoba college and head of the cereal and plant research work there. If a fund such as that

suggested in this motion were set up to encourage other young farm boys and girls to follow this type of work I think it would prove to be very desirable.
Just recently we had in this house an announcement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we have now what is known as Selkirk 15B rust-resistant wheat available in small quantities to farmers in Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan at $5 a bushel. In the Winnipeg Free Press a couple of days ago I noticed a report to the effect that there is a big demand for this same wheat across the border in the United States at $100 a bushel, and that it is not available there. This gives a little idea of the value of research work of this kind.
The losses from rust in the western prairie provinces have been very great in the past. Back in 1935 I think the losses amounted to over $30 million; but, through research, losses last year amounted to approximately $8 million. As I say, through research these losses are becoming less year by year. Now with the introduction of this Selkirk 15B rust-resistant wheat the losses will be still smaller.
I think it is commendable that a fund of this kind should be set up to permit research work on plants and cereals in the universities. In view of the fact that this money has accumulated from the grain producers of the prairie provinces, I think it is proper that it should be spent to the benefit of the grain producers of those provinces. I believe the suggestion in the amendment to divide the money among the farm unions of the prairie provinces would just create a lot of trouble.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext: In what way?

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP SCHOLARSHIPS THROUGH INVESTMENT OF UNDISTRIBUTED BALANCES IN HANDS OP WHEAT BOARD
speechtext: The idea might be commendable, but we have many farm organizations in western Canada; and I would not want to be a member of any board which had to decide how that money should be divided. If that money could be divided without any trouble the idea might be commendable. I believe the idea of setting up a fund to give to boys and girls from the farms of the prairie provinces scholarships in the colleges of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in order to follow this class of work of research and the like, is highly commendable. Therefore I consider that this motion deserves the support of the members of this house.

-with a great deal of interest, as have the other members of the house. It has certainly served very well the purpose indicated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in that it has resulted in a number of members expressing fully and frankly the views they hold in connection with this matter, which is one of some concern.
My interest in the problem is not a practical one in the sense of my representing a constituency in which live and operate a number of producers who have a direct interest in this fund. My connection with it started when it became my duty some time ago to look through the files and see what had been done about this particular problem in the past. I must say that it was a highly interesting study.
In his remarks the hon. member for Ros-thern suggested that the wheat board, being extremely busy with their business of selling wheat, should not be asked to give consideration to a problem of this kind. To the hon. member and to the house I should like to say that from the files it is evident that the wheat board have taken a real interest in this particular matter and that they have found time to give it considerable study and careful consideration. I believe they have agreed in principle with the suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the interest from these funds should perhaps be used for purposes of education.
However, there is one thing that I think should be made clear, and it is this. Up to the present time the principal consideration has been in connection with the employment of the funds that are realized by way of interest on the principal amounts that have been and are still held for the persons actually entitled to them, namely the producers who are entitled to these participation payments but who, for one reason or another, have not received them.
The system is that the board keep a record of the participation-the deliveries-of the various producers, and they do not consider any of these funds as undistributed until the final payment of the pool has been made. Then the funds are considered as undistributed but are held for six years in the general funds of the board and, of course, are available to the producer whenever he comes forward and -asks for payment.
Then as a result of the amendment to the wheat board act passed by this house at the last session, the act now authorizes the wheat board to pay into a special separate account the amounts which are regarded as undistributed. These funds are still held with the

Wheat Board-Scholarships idea and the hope that some day the person or persons really entitled to those funds, as owners, will come forward and collect them. For that reason no serious consideration has been given to disturbing the principal amount of these funds. However, it is recognized that it would be valuable to find some practical means of employing the moneys that accrue by way of interest to the benefit of producers of western Canada. That is really the problem that has to be solved.
